Here's how investors can dodge the downturn.","keywords":["Investing","Investing Strategy","Stocks","Stock Market"],"articleBody":"US stocks may have already peaked, warns a Morgan Stanley investment chief with a penchant for making successful market predictions. Jim Caron, who's the chief investment officer of Morgan Stanley Investment Management's portfolio solutions group, may want to consider buying a lottery ticket. He became bullish on equities in December 2022 before the S&P 500 rallied 24.2% in 2023, and a few weeks ago, his team downgraded the asset class to neutral — just as stocks took a 3.5% hit after a 10.2% rally in the first quarter. The 32-year market veteran expects the second-quarter slide to continue. And considering how much could go wrong in markets, stocks may take a while before rebounding to record highs. \"We are expecting there to be really sideways price action,\" Caron told Business Insider in a recent interview. \"And sideways, to me, could be — we could get more of a selloff from here.\" While Caron is concerned about stocks' near-term outlook, he shouldn't be considered a bear. The leading mind at Morgan Stanley's $1.5 trillion investment management arm is upbeat about the US economy, reasoning that a recession is unlikely in the next 12 to 18 months since the labor market is strong, consumers are steadily spending, and fiscal stimulus is abundant. But Caron cautioned that there are key risks to that seemingly serene market backdrop, including much firmer-than-expected inflation and stretched valuations relative to earnings. Investors bid up stocks last year as profit growth barely budged, reasoning that steadily slowing inflation and a cooling economy would allow the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates six times or more. Neither has happened, so some in markets are no longer counting on cuts. Although optimism about lower rates was overdone, the pendulum may have swung too far. Caron still expects two cuts in the back half of the year, though that might not be enough to live up to the market's historically high valuation, which is heavily dependent on lower rates. The S&P 500 is trading at a rich forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 20.7x that assumes corporate earnings will rise 11% this year. While profits and margins seem reasonable so far in the Q1 earnings season, Caron doubts earnings will meet the sky-high bar set last quarter, when profit growth more than doubled what analysts expected. \"The starting point — the second- and third-quarter earnings — is just a lot harder to beat,\" Caron said. \"We're not going to beat the surprise, I don't think, that we saw in the first quarter.\" For stocks to rally further, they'll likely have to justify their elevated valuations by posting Q1 earnings that meet and comfortably exceed expectations. There's little room for error. And considering how consistently the S&P 500 rose last quarter, the investment chief believes stocks may need to take a breather and grow into their already-ambitious P/E ratio. \"We were priced to a very optimistic level by the end of the first quarter,\" Caron said. \"And now, reality is sinking in that we still have three more quarters to go and that it might be a little bit of a sideways, choppy environment.\" Unless earnings blow estimates out of the water, the investment chief thinks investors should brace for a market drawdown of at least 5% — and potentially a 10% correction. That would take the S&P 500 down to around 4,730, wiping out its year-to-date gains. \"We're probably early in the corrective phase, so I would suspect that we could get a bit more downside,\" Caron said. If there is a downturn, Caron said he'd expect momentum stocks that led the market to all-time highs to take the biggest hits. Many of those firms are large, belong to the technology sector, and have quality attributes like strong balance sheets, cash flows, pricing power, and margins. The momentum and quality factors are intertwined, Caron said, adding that he'd hold off on investing heavily in those groups until they sell off and become sufficiently discounted. \"Eventually, the quality bit will start to win out,\" Caron said. \"And then what we're going to start to talk about are, 'Hey, these are good companies with good cash flows, and they're trading X% cheaper right now. I think I'm going to start to buy these.'\" Although many investors associate best-of-breed attributes with the tech sector, Caron noted those traits can be found in sectors like energy, financials, healthcare, industrials, and materials. Quality stocks in those less-loved sectors should stand out once markets bottom, he said. Until then, investors should diversify beyond stocks by buying quality yield-producing assets like US Treasurys, investment-grade bonds, and mortgage-backed securities, Caron said. Coupons across duration can work since the yield curve is flat — if not slightly inverted. Fixed income has struggled again this year, as evidenced by rising yields, since interest rate expectations have stayed stubbornly high due to persistent inflation. But eventually, Caron said investors won't be able to resist locking in lofty yields while protecting against downside risk. \"The best cure for high yields is high yields because as yields go higher, it becomes like a high-quality hedge to a downturn in the market,\" Caron said. He continued: \"We've got to see the purge first in order for things to settle, and then for people to recognize that quality and then that value. And I think that's the sequential element of what is going on in markets today.\"","articleSection":"Markets","isAccessibleForFree":false,"hasPart":[{"@type":"WebPageElement","isAccessibleForFree":false,"cssSelector":"[data-lock-content]"}]}
